text: Every tradeoff you've made so far in this course felt obvious at the time, to the people in the room. Hub-and-spoke over a transit gateway, one RTO target over another, a line drawn around which accounts get their own landing zone. Six months later, half of that reasoning is gone. This lesson is about why that happens, and why a short, dated, written record fixes it almost for free.

Here's what it looks like in practice. Someone commits a hub-and-spoke network for blast-radius isolation. Months later, a different engineer looks at git log, sees complexity with no explanation attached, and reverts it to a single flat VNet — because nothing on disk told them why the complexity existed. The constraint disappears along with the "simplification," and nobody notices until the failure mode it was protecting against actually happens.

That's one of two failure modes with the same root cause. Silent reversal removes a constraint because its reasoning was never written down. Re-litigation re-argues an already-settled question from scratch, costing real meeting time with no guarantee the second conversation lands in the same place. Both get worse as tribal knowledge walks out the door — the one person who remembers why eventually leaves the team.

A written record doesn't make the original decision better. It makes it legible to everyone who wasn't there, including your own team six months from now. That means durable reasoning that outlives staff turnover, a record of the alternatives that were considered and rejected, and an honest list of the tradeoffs accepted at the time — downsides included, not hidden.

This pattern has a name: the Architecture Decision Record, described by Michael Nygard in a widely read 2011 post and later listed on ThoughtWorks's public Technology Radar as a practice worth adopting. Next lesson, you'll write a real one — Context, Options Considered, Decision, Consequences — with a full worked example instead of just the theory.
